fields.meaning: Pouring all one's ~ into, full of ~ | Means putting one's feelings into something.
examples: For my mother's birthday, I gave her a sweater I had knitted with all my heart.
We all wrote a letter together, full of gratitude to our teacher.
The children folded a thousand paper cranes as a prayer for peace.
With (all one's) love / strength / irony / wishes
*"Thank you for your heartfelt hospitality."
With all one's heart
fields.explain: Expresses putting a lot of emotion or meaning into an action.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ために (purpose).
→ ～をこめて means “to put into / to be filled with”; it emphasizes the feelings/meaning put into an action or object.
2) Often used with words such as 気持ち／愛／感謝.
→ It means “with all…”, “putting all one's … into it”.
3) Not used for practical purposes.
→ If it is a clear purpose of an action, use ～ために／～ように.
meaning_vi: With all…, putting… into
explain: Used for creative/expressive actions: writing, speaking, giving, making, singing, praying…
The noun-modifying form Nを込めたN₂ is often seen in written language/advertising.
Not used with concrete nouns in the sense of “stuffing” unless it is the original meaning of the 動詞「込める」.
Expresses formality and sincerity; suited to positive/ceremonial contexts.
examples: 1. 心を込めて料理を作りました。
I cooked with all my heart.
2. 感謝を込めて花を贈ります。
I send these flowers with gratitude.
3. 平和への祈りを込めて灯りをともした。
We lit the lights with a prayer for peace.
4. 愛を込めた手作りの弁当。
A homemade bento made with love.
5. 彼は怒りを込めてそう言った。
He said so with anger.
6. 一筆一筆に思いを込めて書きました。
I put my feelings into every single brushstroke. meaning_vi: Pouring all, with all, full of ～ ⏐ explain: Putting one's thoughts, feelings and emotions into something. ⏐ examples: 1. 感謝の気持ちをこめて編んだマフラーです。
This is a scarf knitted with heartfelt gratitude.
2. 愛をこめてカードを贈る。
Sending a card full of love.
3. 心をこめる → 心がこもる → 心のこもった手紙
A heartfelt letter.
mistakes: Using it with concrete nouns in a grammatical sense → wrong meaning (e.g., “砂糖を込めてコーヒーを入れる” is unnatural; it should be 砂糖を入れて).
Confusing it with ～をもって: that one marks a formal means and carries no emotion.
Forgetting the noun-modifying form ～を込めたN: it often appears in reading comprehension.

examples: This shop is popular, mainly among students.
Tomorrow, I'll build the schedule around the meeting.
A strong earthquake was observed, centered on the Kanto region.
Economic recovery is lagging, especially among small and medium-sized businesses.
An event centered on children will be held.
The number of tourists increases, mainly in the fall.
fields.explain:
Used with a noun that serves as the “axis” around which an activity, scope or target unfolds.
Common in the news: 地域・年齢層・時間帯+ を中心に.
“～を中心として” is more formal than “～を中心に”; “～を中心にして” emphasizes the process of revolving around something.
The noun-modifying variant “Nを中心としたN₂” is very natural in writing.
Not used to express volition/requests; it mainly describes facts/directions.

• Taking N as the center/core/main element: organizations, plans and activities revolve around N.
• Mainly N: the main target group, main area, key content.
• Spatial/temporal scope “around N”: concentrated in/around the area N or the point in time N.
• Nuance: objective, describes distribution/focus; suited to announcements, news and reports.
• Different from “only about N”: emphasizes a center-satellite relationship, not “on the topic of N”.
fields.notes:
• Can have a spatial meaning (東京を中心に), refer to a group of people (高齢者を中心に), or to time (夏を中心に).
• In headlines/advertising, を is often omitted: 週末中心にセール開催.
• “中心に据える/据えた” is an advanced expression: placing N as the axis.
• Avoid overusing it with abstract nouns that cannot clearly be a “center”.
meaning_vi: Taking ~ as the center
explain: ◎ Expresses the idea "taking ~ as the central position" or "regarding ~ as the most important".
examples: 1. 彼を中心に新しいバンドができた。
A new band was formed with him at its center.
2. ４月２２日は「地球の日」で、この日を中心に各地でさまざまなイベントが行われます。
April 22 is "Earth Day," so various events will be held in many places before, after and on that day. | Variants: ～を中心として・を中心にして
mistakes: Confusing it with ～をめぐって: the latter emphasizes disputes; ～を中心に only indicates distribution/focus.
Using it with verbs: incorrect. This pattern attaches directly to nouns.
Using it to state volition/requests: unnatural (the pattern is descriptive).
Forgetting the noun-modifying variant “Nを中心としたN₂”, which often appears in JLPT reading comprehension.

fields.explain:
Used mainly in casual speech. In formal written language, ～ということだ／～そうだ (伝聞) is used.
The intonation rises at the end of the sentence when it is a confirmation question: ～んだって？
～んだって is not used to state a personal opinion; its function is reporting.
Combine it with っていう話／って聞いた to emphasize the source: ～って聞いたんだって (A said they heard…)

- Expresses indirect reporting: “I heard / someone said that…”. The spoken equivalent of ～そうだ／～ということだ when used for reporting.
- Casual, conversational nuance; shows that the speaker is not asserting anything with certainty but only passing on information they heard.
- Can be used as a question to confirm information: ～んだって？
fields.notes:
• Adding the source: ～んだって、ニュースで（友だちが／先生が）。
• Negative/past forms stay as they are: 来ないんだって／行ったんだって。
• Emphasizing doubt: 本当なんだって？／マジなんだって？
mistakes: Confusing it with ～だって (because/even). “雨なんだって” = I heard it's raining; “雨だって” = even rain… a different meaning.
Using it in formal language: switch to ～ということだ／～そうだ.
Forgetting “な” before nouns/な-adjectives: 有名んだって × correct: 有名なんだって。

rows: Neutral, can be used in writing
<ruby>中止<rt>ちゅうし</rt></ruby>になるということだ。
Contracted form of と<ruby>言<rt>い</rt></ruby>っている
Very colloquial; ～んだって includes the explanatory のだ

fields.meaning: On the one hand…, on the other… | More and more…, keeps on…
examples: This system is fair, but the procedures are complicated.
Cities are convenient, but on the other hand they have little nature.
The population of young people is decreasing. On the other hand, the number of elderly people is increasing.
On the one hand, we need to lower prices; on the other, we must also maintain quality.
Company A is increasing its sales overseas, while struggling in the domestic market.
He is sociable, but he also values his time alone.
fields.explain:
Used to balance information and show a multifaceted view; suits an objective style.
Should be used when the two clauses share the same topic or the same scope of comparison/contrast.
“その一方で” stands at the beginning of the sentence that follows to present the other side, avoiding repetition of the subject.
“一方” is not used for pure listing; there must be some contrast/difference.

• Presents two opposing or different sides/aspects of the same issue/subject: “on the one hand …, on the other hand …”.
• Contrasts two phenomena/groups: “while …, …”. They do not have to contradict each other completely; it just emphasizes the contrast.
• “その一方で” is used as a transition phrase in the following sentence, adding contrary information to balance the argument.
• Formal nuance; often used in journalism, reports and argumentative writing.
• Note the distinction from “一方だ” (one-way progression); “一方” here does NOT mean “more and more”.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ていく／～てくる.
→ ～一方だ expresses a change in only one direction.
2) Often has a negative meaning or describes something beyond one's control.
→ Example: 悪化する一方だ.
3) Not used for controlled positive changes.
→ For a development plan, another pattern is usually used.
mistakes: Confusing it with “一方だ” when you want to say “more and more”. “一方” (contrast) does not express a tendency.
Dropping “で” after “一方” when connecting: both “一方、” and “一方で、” are correct; choose according to the context.
Using it when the two clauses have no topical connection → the sentence becomes disjointed and loses its logic.
Using it for cause and effect → wrong nuance; “一方” expresses contrast, not cause.

rows: Formal; used within the same topic or for two related phenomena
<ruby>都心<rt>としん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby><ruby>一方<rt>いっぽう</rt></ruby>、<ruby>家賃<rt>やちん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>い。
Stronger “flip side” nuance; usually the same subject
<ruby>便利<rt>べんり</rt></ruby>な<ruby>反面<rt>はんめん</rt></ruby>、<ruby>騒音<rt>そうおん</rt></ruby>が<ruby>多<rt>おお</rt></ruby>い。
Emphasizes the symmetry between two different targets

More and more, a one-way tendency
Not a contrast; only indicates the degree of increase/decrease

examples: I finished writing the report in a single night.
It is a craft item that an artisan spent many years creating.
Lifting heavy boxes is dangerous.
To launch a project.
Due to soaring costs, the plan is to raise prices.
fields.explain:
Attaches directly after the continuative form (Vます). Note how the meaning changes depending on the base verb: 書く→書き上げる (completion); 上げる carries the nuance of “up / all the way”.
Many compound words are fixed and need to be memorized as set phrases: 仕上げる／見上げる／立ち上げる／積み上げる。
Do not confuse it with ～てあげる (doing something for someone). ～上げる, written with the kanji “上げる”, indicates result/direction/increase.

- Meaning 1 (result/completion): Expresses doing something to the end, completing a process that produces a tangible product/result. Commonly seen: 仕上げる, 仕上がる (intransitive), 書き上げる, 作り上げる, 立ち上げる.
- Meaning 2 (direction/upward movement): Moving an object/the body upward: 持ち上げる, 立ち上げる（start up, set up）.
- Meaning 3 (raising/pushing up): Raising a level/value: 値段を引き上げる, スピードを上げる.
- Nuance: decisive, strong, sometimes implying effort to produce a result.
fields.notes:
• Many IT/business terms: 立ち上げ（launching a project/system）, 立ち上げる（launch）。
• “仕上げる/仕上がる” is a very common pair for “finishing”.
• In economics: 値上げ（price increase）, 引き上げ（raising a level）, 金利を引き上げる。
mistakes: Confusing it with ～てあげる: 書いてあげる ≠ 書き上げる. The first means “write for (someone)”, the second means “finish writing”.
Mixing up intransitive and transitive verbs: 出来上がる（intransitive） vs 作り上げる（transitive）。
Choosing the wrong nuance compared with ～終える: the JLPT often sets a trap with “読み上げる” (read aloud) vs “読み終える” (finish reading).

rows: Strong sense of direction: “up / all the way”
Neutral, only ending; no nuance of “raising up”
Doing something to the end, thoroughly
Emphasizes thoroughness/ending; a different range of meaning from “up”

examples: This camera is not only light but also easy to operate.
Not only does he break his promises, but he also makes nothing but excuses.
The location is convenient, and on top of that, the rent is reasonable.
On top of being an expert, this person has plenty of hands-on experience.
It's raining, and on top of that, there's even thunder.
This case not only takes time but also involves a lot of procedures.
fields.explain:
Used to emphasize the “accumulation” of characteristics; avoid using it for a direct cause-and-effect relationship.
Suited to formal language; in casual spoken language it can be replaced with “それに/しかも”.
Avoid combining two clauses pointing in opposite directions (good + bad).

• “Not only … but also …”: adds a characteristic/condition in the same direction (good → better, bad → worse).
• The two clauses must share the same direction of evaluation (both positive or both negative).
• More formal nuance than “それに/しかも/さらに”; used a lot in writing/reports/introductions.
fields.notes:
• Written language often uses the pair: Aである上に、Bである。This creates a formal, consistent feel.
• In advertising/PR, “A上にB” makes the message more persuasive when both A and B are positive.
• When adding a third clause, use “その上/さらに” to avoid repeating “上に”.
explain: ◎ Means "Not only that".
examples: 1. さくらさんは頭がいいうえに、スポーツもできる。
Sakura is not only smart but also good at sports.
2. 今日バスに乗り遅れたうえに、忘れ物もしてしまって、最悪な一日だった。

meaning_vi: States one fact, then states another fact that heightens the positive or negative evaluation.

examples: 1. 彼の妹は美人の上に性格も良い/成績優秀な上、スポーツもよくできる。

On top of that, the print is small, so it is hard for children to read. meaning_vi: Not only… moreover ⏐ explain: Adds something with the idea that it has the same tendency as the preceding fact (besides this good point there is another good point, or a bad point added to a bad thing).
In the second clause, sentences that act on the listener, such as commands, prohibitions, requests, invitations…, cannot be used. ⏐ examples: 1. 彼は仕事ができる上に優しい。
He is not only good at his job but also kind.
2. 昨日は寒かった上に、風が強かった。
Yesterday it was not only cold but also windy.
mistakes: Combining opposite directions: “安い上に味が悪い” → contradictory nuance; use “が/けれど” instead.
Dropping “である” with N/na-adjectives in formal language → unnatural: “専門家上に” → incorrect.
Using it to state a direct cause → wrong function; “上に” adds information, it does not mean because/therefore.

examples: Since breaking up with him, I've thrown myself into my work.
Since moving, I've had more interaction with my neighbors.

Since moving
fields.explain:
Used in news, biographies and personal stories.
Often used with ずっと／一度も～ない to emphasize continuity/absoluteness.
The second clause is usually in the present or the present perfect in Japanese (～ている).

• Since … (until now). Emphasizes duration/continuation.
• The second clause describes an ongoing state or a change that has lasted until the present.
• Not used with direct commands/volition.
fields.notes:
• Besides people/things, the reference point can be a social event: コロナ禍以来.
• Not used with a repeated action as a vague reference point: X 彼に会う以来.
• The second clause is sometimes a one-time change but implies that it continues: 吸わなくなった（and it is still that way now）. meaning_vi: Since, ever since　～ ⏐ explain: Indicates something that has continued from a point in time in the past up to now, after a certain action.
The second clause does not use sentences expressing things that happen only once. ⏐ examples: 1. 日本に来て以来、母の料理を食べていない。
Since coming to Japan, I haven't eaten my mother's cooking.
2. 入学以来、一度も授業を休んでいない。
Since entering school, I haven't missed a single class.
mistakes: Mixing it up with 以降 in announcements about the future: X 来週以来 → it should be 来週以降.
The second clause expresses an instantaneous event that does not last: X 結婚して以来、昨日パーティーをした。
Wrong vague reference point (repeated action): X 彼に会う以来 → should be: 彼に会って以来.

rows: Only indicates sequence; does not suggest continuity.
<ruby>昼寝<rt>ひるね</rt></ruby>してから、<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>した。

fields.name: ～向き（suitability）
examples: A design suited to children / A course suited to beginners
These days, when it comes to occupations, you can no longer say that a job is suited to men or suited to women.
Traditional Japanese houses are built to suit the summer.
This area gets little rain, so it is unsuitable for growing rice.
fields.explain: Indicates suitability for a particular purpose or target.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～向け (intended for).
→ ～向き means “suitable for a target/purpose”; it emphasizes suitability.
2) Often used to evaluate suitability.
→ Example: 初心者向き, 子ども向き.
3) It is not necessarily something made specifically for that target.
→ If it means “made to serve a target” (in terms of intended release), ～向け is usually used.
